entries.title: Enshrined Conflict: The Paradox of the Yasukuni Shrine - Brown Political Review
entries.paragraph_1: The 1946 Tokyo War Crimes Trials , carried out by the Allied powers during postwar occupation, marked one of the first attempts to reckon with the atrocities committed by the Japanese Army during the Second World War. 28 men, many of whom were architects of the war, were indicted on charges of “Class A” war crimes for directing aggression that led to crimes against humanity. The trials represented an initial but important effort to reconcile a violence-filled past waged across East Asia. However, the legacy of the trials became far more complicated 30 years later, when 14 Class A criminals were enshrined in the Yasukuni shrine—a monument in the heart of Tokyo meant to honor those who gave their lives in service to the Japanese military. Since then, the shrine has been the subject of heated debate and constant controversy. After all, the 14 men were responsible for millions of deaths. The shrine also honors 2.5 million others who gave their lives in service of Japan throughout history, many of whom never saw the battlefield. As such, visits have been justified as an important remembrance for all of those who gave their life for the nation, a remembrance that should not be diluted by the inclusion of a small percentage of war criminals. At first glance, the shrine seems to propose a straightforward moral tension: how should a nation honor sacrifice while acknowledging horrific wrongdoing in its past? But this framing is incomplete. Controversy around Yasukuni persists because it attempts to serve two legitimate but ultimately opposing purposes. As a Shinto landmark, it seeks to nonjudgementally honor the dead and provide the living with a means to fulfill religious obligations; as a political symbol, it appears to affirm a hypernationalist, negationist, and revisionist view of history that at best denies and at worst glorifies past atrocities. As long as the shrine is asked to serve this dual function, any conflict surrounding it will remain irresolvable.
entries.paragraph_2: Yasukuni—which translates to “to preserve peace for the entire nation”—is a Shinto shrine, placing it within a religious framework that does not and cannot make moral distinctions between the dead. Shinto is Japan’s indigenous religion , centered around the worship of divine spirits. The shrine was established in 1869 by Emperor Meiji in the wake of a civil war to honor those who died and gave their souls for the Emperor. In Shinto belief, the dead become Kami , a rough equivalent to the word “spirit” or “deity.” Crucially, Shinto followers see death as inherently tragic no matter what, and believe there is no evaluative judgment of the dead or delineation into heaven or hell. On the contrary, it is up to the living, through rituals and worship, to ensure a peaceful transition and a fruitful afterlife for all of the dead and to maintain harmony between the living and spiritual realms. Within this logic, the enshrinement of war criminals in Yasukuni is not necessarily a statement on morality, history, or national memory; it is simply the fulfillment of a religious obligation to the communal war dead, regardless of the actions of specific individuals within that group.

entries.paragraph_2: New Delhi [India], November 13 (ANI): India's exports to key Free Trade Agreement (FTA) partners registered strong growth during April-September FY27, with shipments to Singapore surging 103 per cent, Malaysia rising 83 per cent and ASEAN countries recording a 58 per cent increase, according to data presented by the Ministry of Commerce and Industry on Friday. The data, presented during a press conference addressed by Commerce Secretary Rajesh Agrawal, highlighted India's expanding trade partnerships and recent developments in free trade agreements, including the implementation of the India-New Zealand FTA and progress under the India-European Free Trade Association (EFTA) agreement. According to the ministry, India's exports to Singapore more than doubled to USD 11.07 billion during April-September FY27 from USD 5.45 billion in the corresponding period last year. Exports to ASEAN countries increased to USD 28.06 billion from USD 17.75 billion, while shipments to Malaysia rose to USD 5.58 billion from USD 3.05 billion. Similarly, exports to Sri Lanka increased 73 per cent to USD 3.94 billion, while shipments to Oman rose 47 per cent to USD 3.29 billion. Exports to Japan increased 40 per cent to USD 4.10 billion, while shipments to South Korea grew 24 per cent to USD 3.91 billion.

entries.title: South Korea Backs Naval Push Toward Hormuz as Iran Warns
entries.paragraph_1: South Korea's Cabinet approved a plan Tuesday to expand the operating area of its Cheonghae anti-piracy naval unit from the Gulf of Aden to waters south of Oman, about 650 kilometers, or 400 miles, from the Strait of Hormuz, and Iran has since warned Seoul twice against taking part in what it calls U.S. aggression. The government says the unit will not join the war and will stay under South Korean command. The motion now goes to the National Assembly, where the ruling Democratic Party holds a majority but smaller left-leaning parties in the broader ruling camp have objected.
entries.paragraph_2: The plan would roughly double the unit's operating radius, to about 1,930 kilometers, pushing it northeast into the Arabian Sea toward the Omani port of Duqm. It would add 75 personnel, a 30-member explosive ordnance disposal team and 45 people to operate a P-8 Poseidon maritime patrol aircraft, along with uncrewed mine-countermeasure equipment. The Gulf of Oman, which adjoins the strait, is not included in the proposed area. entries.paragraph_1: Il protocollo di aggiornamento 3.0 dell’ Area di libero scambio Cina-ASEAN entrerà in vigore il 1° dicembre. Lo ha annunciato la Xinhua oggi, secondo giorno del vertice dell’ASEAN che proseguirà fino al 17 novembre e vede riuniti i leader dei dieci paesi membri oltre ai rappresentanti delle principali nazioni partner, tra cui Stati Uniti, Australia, Giappone e India. Attesa la partecipazione di Donald Trump e del primo ministro indiano Narendra Modi. I punti chiavi da monitorare, secondo il Nikkei :
entries.paragraph_2: Intanto, domenica 15 novembre, Filippine e Australia hanno firmato a Manila un accordo di cooperazione in materia di difesa con l’obiettivo di rafforzare il coordinamento militare bilaterale.Il segretario alla Difesa filippino, Gilberto Teodoro, ha dichiarato che l’intesa consentirà di semplificare l’attuazione dello Status of Visiting Forces Agreement (SOVFA) , riducendo gli adempimenti burocratici necessari per le operazioni congiunte. Secondo Teodoro, l’accordo contribuirà anche a rafforzare la capacità di deterrenza delle Filippine, in particolare nel Mar cinese meridionale.

entries.title: US-China-Russia summit mustn’t become a ‘second Yalta,’ says South Korea’s top diplomat
entries.paragraph_1: South Korea’s foreign minister said a summit between North Korea and the US on the sidelines of this week’s Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit in Shenzhen, China, remains possible but unlikely. Seoul’s top diplomat also said he had conveyed to China that any decisions reached at a potential summit between the leaders of the US, China and Russia must not undermine South Korea’s national interests. Speaking to reporters at the Korean Embassy in Beijing on Saturday, Foreign Minister Cho discussed his meeting with Chinese Foreign Minister Wang Yi the previous day, which lasted about 90 minutes and was followed by a dinner. A senior South Korean Foreign Ministry official said the Chinese side had shared its assessment of the prospects for a North Korea-US summit. “Ultimately, the most important variables are the situation in the US and President Donald Trump’s willingness to hold a summit. Another variable is how receptive North Korea will be,” the official said. “Taking everything into account, we cannot rule out the possibility under the current circumstances,” the official continued. “We need to be prepared and ensure that our national interests aren’t compromised.” Seoul also conveyed its opposition to a repeat of the 1945 Yalta Conference, at which the major powers decided the postwar international order without involving the countries that were directly affected. “If a US-China-Russia summit takes place, it must not become a ‘second Yalta Conference,’“ the official said. “We’ve made it clear not only to the US but also to China that our national interests cannot be compromised on matters concerning the Korean Peninsula. We made that position abundantly clear again yesterday.” The official said that China understands South Korea’s position that the three powers must not make decisions that would grant North Korea recognition as a nuclear-armed state or thwart efforts to establish a peace regime on the Korean Peninsula. The South Korean delegation also received an update on recent exchanges between China and North Korea. The official said the Chinese side had provided “relatively detailed accounts” of North Korean leader Kim Jong-un’s visit to Dandong on Oct. 24 and Korean Workers’ Party international secretary Kim Song-nam’s visit to China on Nov. 5. “The Chinese side described relations with North Korea as focusing more on economic cooperation than on political matters, and that was very much the impression I came away with,” the official said. Cho said that he had emphasized that peace on the Korean Peninsula was a “vital interest” for South Korea and that Wang had agreed that peace and stability on the peninsula were also in China’s national interest. Regarding bilateral relations, Cho said China had expressed its intention to give President Lee Jae Myung a special welcome during his visit for the APEC summit. With the 35th anniversary of diplomatic relations approaching next year, the two countries agreed that discussions would continue at the working level about concrete cooperation projects with a meaningful public impact that can be announced at the APEC summit next week. The talks also covered longstanding issues raised by Korea, including Chinese structures installed in the Yellow Sea. The Chinese said they would make a good-faith effort to address those issues. Cho said the two sides also agreed on the need to reduce negative sentiment among their respective populations and move bilateral relations in a mutually positive direction.

entries.paragraph_1: The US atomic bombings of Hiroshima and Nagasaki in 1945 were war crimes against civilians, so the US government ought to compensate the Korean victims, an international people’s tribunal has ruled. The International People’s Tribunal on the 1945 Atomic Bombings found in a preliminary judgment on Sunday that the US bombings of the two Japanese cities in August 1945 constituted war crimes, violating international legal prohibitions on direct attacks on civilians even during total war. The bombings killed approximately 210,000 people, including 40,000 Koreans.
entries.paragraph_2: The tribunal concluded that the US government is obligated to compensate the Korean victims. The Organizing Committee of the International People’s Tribunal on the 1945 Atomic Bombings and the Korean civic group Solidarity for Peace and Reunification of Korea (SPARK) convened the tribunal from Nov. 13 to 15 at Hanshin University’s Graduate School of Theology in the Suyu neighborhood of Seoul’s Gangbuk District. As the tribunal was organized by civilians, its judgment is not legally binding. Nevertheless, it marks the first attempt in the world to put the US government on trial for its use of atomic bombs. In its judgment, the panel of judges found that “atomic bombings constituted war crimes and crimes against humanity under customary international law as it stood in 1945.” “The atomic bombings constituted war crimes, as the wanton destruction of cities was not justifiable by military necessity. They also constituted crimes against humanity, as they were planned acts of mass killing directed against civilians,” the judges found. The judges also concluded that “the United States is under an obligation under international law to compensate Korean atomic bomb victims for the harm they suffered” — and, indeed, continue to suffer — “as a result of the atomic bombings.” The judges found that the bombings violated prohibitions against direct attacks on civilians, indiscriminate attacks and methods of warfare that “would violate laws of humanity and public conscience.” They also concluded that the bombings exceeded what was necessary for legitimate military purposes and violated the requirements of necessity and proportionality. Twelve Korean plaintiffs participated in the proceedings, including seven individuals who survived direct exposure to the bombings, as well as four second-generation victims and one third-generation victim with conditions attributed to their parents’ and grandparents’ radiation exposure. Among them was Shim Jin-tae, head of the Hapcheon chapter of the Korea Atomic Bombs Victim Association.
